title: Gargi: on what is everything woven?
hookLine: a woman stands up in a courtyard full of men and asks a child's endless why, all the way up to Brahman
tomorrow: the father of 'you are that' stands up. what does he ask?
last: THE SELF IS THE SELF IS BEYOND HUNGER, GRIEF AND DEATH HUNGER, GRIEF AND DEATH.

lines: ALL THE WAY TO THE TOP.
cards: Why is it raining? Because of the clouds. Why are there clouds?
Because of the water. Why is there water? A child can keep that chain going until the grown-up says, because I said so.
Now put that chain in a royal courtyard, where a woman has just stood up among the learned men of the Kuru and Panchala lands.
Her name is Gargi Vachaknavi, and she's about to ask Yajnavalkya why, again and again, all the way to the top.

teach.b: Yajnavalkya, she says, everything here is woven, back and forth, on water. On what, then, is water woven? Weaving is her picture: threads running lengthwise and crosswise, each held by another.

teach.h: WIND, AIR, SUN, MOON, STARS, GODS.
teach.b: On wind, Gargi, he says. On what is wind woven? On the worlds of the middle air.
Then the worlds of the heavenly musicians. Of the sun. Of the moon.
Of the stars. Of the gods. Of Indra.
Of Prajapati, the lord of creatures. And on what are the worlds of Prajapati woven? On the worlds of Brahman.
On what, she asks, are the worlds of Brahman woven? Here he stops her.
Gargi, don't ask too much, or your head will fall off. You are asking beyond a deity one shouldn't ask beyond. And Gargi falls silent.

teach.h: BRAHMAN: WHAT ALL IS WOVEN ON.
teach.b: Brahman, the ultimate reality, is what everything is woven on. Every answer so far named a thing, and you can always ask what holds a thing.
But what holds everything isn't one more thread in the cloth. Asking what it's woven on is like asking what's north of the North Pole.
Later, in the Gita, Krishna uses the same picture: all this is strung on me, like pearls on a thread. Gargi isn't wrong to ask; she's found the edge of the question.
Every Hindu parent eventually hears the small version: who made God? And who made that? This is the old answer: God isn't one more thing that needs a maker.
And Gargi isn't finished. In two days, she'll stand up again, armed.

how: Hindu tradition remembers Gargi Vachaknavi as a philosopher of the Vedic age, and her questions to Yajnavalkya are studied as part of the Brihadaranyaka's great debate.

o: a goddess who weaves the worlds together
the woman who asked what all is woven on
the queen who hosted Janaka's debate

games.q: what's woven on what — tap the pairs.
p: woven on the worlds of Brahman
the woman who asked, on what?

s: Gargi asks her questions only once in the debate
she falls silent here, but she stands up again later in the debate.
he stops her: don't ask too much, or your head will fall off.
Gargi's picture for the world is weaving
everything woven, back and forth, on something else.

games.q: you're Gargi. you've asked what water, wind, sun, stars, gods and Prajapati are woven on, and got an answer every time. what's your next question?
o: on what are the worlds of Brahman woven?
games.why: she asks, and Yajnavalkya stops her: don't ask too much, Gargi, or your head will fall off. she falls silent, for now.

practice: Feel what holds you: you on the seat, the seat on the floor, the floor on the building, the building on the earth, the earth held in space, with a breath at each step.
When you reach the last one you can name, don't push for another. Rest right there, at the edge, where the answers stop and you're still held.

wordCard.voice: Gargi. The woman who asked what everything is woven on, ota and prota, warp and weft, until the answers ran out at the edge of the question.

orig.note: Sanskrit ota and prota: woven lengthwise and crosswise, warp and weft, from vā, to weave.

carryVoice: Carry this: everything is woven on Brahman. Tomorrow, an old friend from the Chandogya steps up. That's day three hundred seventy-seven.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 7.7 (all this is strung on me like pearls on a thread)
